faq.question: What is an employment verification letter?
faq.answer: It is a factual confirmation of employment details such as employer, job title, dates, and current status. The requester and employer policy determine the accepted fields and delivery method.

faq.question: Does it need salary information?
faq.answer: Not always. Include compensation only when the requester requires it and the employer is authorized to disclose it.

faq.question: Can an employee write the letter?
faq.answer: An employee can request or draft a proposed version, but a requester may require verification from HR, a supervisor, payroll, or an authorized verification service.

faq.question: What if the employer uses an automated verification service?
faq.answer: Follow that process. A platform-generated verification may be more acceptable than a manually signed letter.

faq.question: Does a verification letter guarantee approval?
faq.answer: No. It confirms facts; it does not control a landlord, lender, employer, agency, or other reviewer’s decision.

faq.question: Can ApprovalPrep send employment verification letter for me?
faq.answer: No. ApprovalPrep is self-service. You review, download, and send your own materials.

faq.question: Should I use original documents?
faq.answer: Usually keep originals and send copies unless the requester’s current instructions specifically require originals or an official verification channel.

faq.question: What if the requester asks for something different?
faq.answer: Follow the requester’s current instructions and ask for clarification. This page is a preparation framework, not a substitute for the reviewer’s rules.

/landlord-reference-letter.heading: Landlord Reference Letter
/landlord-reference-letter.lead: A landlord reference letter is a current or former landlord's signed statement about one tenancy: the address, the dates, the rent, the payment record, and whether they would rent to you again. Build one in the browser below, from either side of the request.
/landlord-reference-letter.shortAnswer: Ask a landlord for facts they can check against their own ledger — dates, rent, late count, notice history — instead of praise. A checkable letter survives a screening review; a warm one gets skimmed and set aside.
decisionContext: This page helps you decide which of three documents your leasing office actually wants, and then produce it. Reference letter, verification form, and rent ledger get used interchangeably in listings and they answer different questions.

It also helps you decide what to ask your landlord for. A landlord who is asked for a glowing reference often produces something vague; a landlord who is asked to confirm five specific facts usually produces something a screener can use.

Where the payment record is not clean, the decision is whether to name it. Naming it costs less than it appears to, because a screening report will show it anyway and an unexplained gap between two documents reads worse than a disclosed late payment.
The generator is free and stays free. The paid Rental Application Kit is for the case where you want the editable file and the rest of the rental packet in one download.
whoFor: Renters applying for an apartment who have been asked for a reference from a previous landlord.
Renters with a thin or interrupted rental history who need the record explained rather than hidden.
Landlords and small property managers who have been asked to write a reference and want to stay inside fair-housing lines.
Anyone who was handed a rental verification form and cannot tell whether a letter would satisfy it.
value: A working generator that produces finished text in the browser, rather than a page describing what a letter should contain.
Three versions covering the three real situations: the landlord writes it, the tenant asks for it, or the management company can only confirm facts.
A comparison table that settles which document was actually requested before you spend a week chasing the wrong one.
Fair-housing boundaries stated plainly, so a landlord writing a favour does not create a problem for themselves.
whatYouGet: A browser-only generator producing three distinct documents from one set of answers.
A short template and a second template for the case where the payment record is not clean.
A field list to send your landlord so they confirm a record instead of reconstructing one.
A review checklist to run before the letter is sent.
Primary sources on tenant screening and fair housing.
useCases: The leasing office asked for a landlord reference and gave you no format.
Your previous property manager says company policy bars them from giving a reference.
You were late on rent twice and need the letter to address it rather than avoid it.
You are the landlord, a former tenant has asked for a reference, and you want to help without overstepping.
You need the reference and a completed verification form for the same application.
prepBrief: Tenant's full legal name as it appears on the lease
Full rental address including unit number
Landlord or property manager's name and business contact
Tenancy start date and end date, or a statement that the tenancy is current
Monthly rent amount and whether it changed during the tenancy
Number of late payments and any notices served
Condition of the unit at move-out and whether the deposit was returned
A direct answer on whether the landlord would rent to the tenant again
commonMistakes: Writing the letter yourself and asking the landlord only to sign it. Leasing agents read a lot of these and a tenant-voiced letter is obvious; ask the landlord to put the opinion sentence in their own words.

Using a friend, a relative, or a personal cell number in place of the real landlord. The reference gets called, and a reference that does not check out is worse for the application than no reference at all.
Asking for praise instead of facts. A letter that says a tenant was wonderful and gives no dates, no rent figure, and no payment record settles nothing a screener needs settled.
Hiding a late payment the ledger will show anyway. A reference that says the record was spotless next to a screening report showing two late months damages everything else in the packet.
Letting the landlord mention children, a medical situation, an immigration status, or a religion. It does not help the tenant and it exposes the landlord to a fair-housing complaint.
reviewChecklist: Every date matches the lease, not your memory of it.
The rent figure matches what you actually paid, including any mid-tenancy increase.
The landlord's phone number and email are ones that will be answered during business hours.
Nothing in the letter mentions family, health, disability, religion, or national origin.
The letter names one tenancy and one address, not a general character reference.
steps: Ask the leasing office what they will accept: a signed letter, a completed verification form, or a phone call. Some accept only one, and building the wrong one costs you a week.
Ask your landlord early, and ask in writing. A landlord who is asked by text on a Friday afternoon writes a worse letter than one who gets a written request with the facts already listed.
Send the landlord the facts you already know — address, dates, rent — so they are confirming a record rather than reconstructing one from memory.
Let the landlord write the opinion sentence in their own words. A letter where every sentence sounds like the tenant wrote it reads as coached.
Check every date and amount against your lease and your payment records before the letter goes out. A rent figure that is $50 off is the kind of thing a screener notices.
Ask for it on letterhead or from the landlord's business email address, and keep a copy of what was sent and when.

faq.question: What should a landlord reference letter include?
faq.answer: The rental address, the tenancy dates, the monthly rent, the payment record, any notices served, the condition of the unit at move-out, a direct answer on whether the landlord would rent to the tenant again, and the landlord's business contact so the reference can be verified.

faq.question: Can I write my own landlord reference letter?
faq.answer: You can draft it and send it to your landlord to correct and sign, and doing so usually gets you a faster reply. What you cannot do is sign it yourself and submit it as a reference — a leasing office treats that as your own statement, which is a different and much weaker thing.

faq.question: What if my old landlord will not write one?
faq.answer: Ask instead for the facts-only confirmation, which many management companies are permitted to send when a full reference is not. If that is also refused, substitute the evidence you control: cancelled rent cheques, bank statements showing the transfers, the signed lease, and the return of your deposit.

faq.question: Is a landlord reference letter the same as rental verification?
faq.answer: No. A reference letter is written prose with an opinion in it. A rental verification form is a fixed set of fields the landlord completes with no opinion, usually on a form the new landlord or housing agency supplies. Some applications ask for one, some for the other, and a few for both.

faq.question: How long should it be?
faq.answer: One page, and usually three or four sentences. A leasing agent reading dozens of applications gives it perhaps twenty seconds, so the dates, the rent, and the payment record should all be visible without scrolling.

faq.question: Does a strong reference letter guarantee I get the apartment?
faq.answer: No. It settles one question among several. Income, credit, occupancy limits, pets, and the timing of other applications all sit outside what any reference letter can influence.

/rental-verification-form.heading: Rental Verification Form
/rental-verification-form.lead: A rental verification form is the fixed field sheet a new landlord or housing agency sends to a previous landlord: dates, rent, balance owed, late count, notices, would-rent-again. Complete one below — with the tenant authorization that is the reason most of them come back blank.
/rental-verification-form.shortAnswer: Send the authorization with the form, not after it. A previous landlord who receives a verification request without written tenant consent is usually instructed to ignore it, which is why these forms sit unanswered for weeks.
decisionContext: This page helps you decide what to send, in what order, so that a verification request is actually answered rather than filed. The order matters more than the wording: authorization first, in the same message as the form.

It also helps you decide whether a verification form is what was asked for at all. A leasing office that says 'rental verification' sometimes means a reference letter and sometimes means a rent ledger, and the three take different amounts of time to obtain.

For a landlord being asked to complete one, the decision is what to answer and what to leave blank. Anything that cannot be supported from the ledger should be left blank; a guess that is later contradicted hurts the tenant more than a blank does.
The generator is free. The paid Rental Application Kit is the editable download for people who want the verification, the cover letter, and the rest of the rental packet in one file set.
whoFor: Renters whose application is on hold because a previous landlord has not returned a verification.
Renters who were handed a blank verification form and no instructions on who completes it.
Landlords and property managers asked to verify a former tenant and unsure what they may disclose.
Anyone documenting rent history for a mortgage file or a housing agency rather than a lease.

A four-way comparison that settles which document the requester meant before you chase the wrong one.

Your old management company has ignored two verification requests.
A mortgage underwriter has asked for 12 months of documented rent history.
A housing agency needs a previous tenancy verified before a voucher can be issued.
You are the landlord, a verification arrived, and you want to know what you may and may not answer.
prepBrief: Tenant's full legal name and any co-tenant named on the lease
Full rental address including unit number
Previous landlord or management company name, phone, and email or fax
Requester's name, organization, and where the completed form should be returned
Lease start date and lease end date, or current-tenancy status
Monthly rent, and whether rent was ever increased during the tenancy
Any outstanding balance, and any amount charged against the deposit
Number of late payments, notices served, and whether an eviction was ever filed
The tenant's signed and dated authorization to release the rental history
commonMistakes: Sending the form without the tenant's signed authorization. This is the single largest cause of an unanswered verification, and it is fully preventable.
Letting the tenant carry the form. A verification that passes through the applicant's hands loses most of its value; it has to travel from the previous landlord's office to the requester.
Using your own form when the requester supplied one. Housing agencies and underwriters often cannot accept a substitute, and the file is returned as incomplete.
Answering fields from memory. A landlord who guesses at a late count and is later contradicted by their own ledger has damaged the tenant they were trying to help.
Sending it with no deadline and no return path. A request that does not say where to send the answer or by when is the easiest thing in a records inbox to defer.
reviewChecklist: The tenant's authorization is signed and dated, and names the same address as the form.
The rental address on the form matches the lease exactly, unit number included.
There is a return-by date and a working return address, fax, or email on the form.
Every field the landlord answered can be supported from the rent ledger.
The form went from the previous landlord to the requester, not by way of the tenant.
steps: Ask the requester which form they want. If they have their own, use theirs; a substitute form is a common reason a file is returned as incomplete.
Have the tenant sign the authorization first. Send it in the same message as the form, not as a follow-up after the landlord has already ignored the request.
Address the request to the management office, not to an individual leasing agent who may have moved on. Include the property address in the subject line so it can be found by unit.
Give the landlord a deadline and a return path. A form with no return-by date and no fax or email goes to the bottom of the pile.
Ask the landlord to answer from the ledger. Anything they cannot support from their records should be left blank rather than guessed.
Follow up once by phone after 5 days. The most common outcome is not refusal, it is that the email went to a shared inbox nobody reads.

faq.question: What is a rental verification form?
faq.answer: A fixed-field request sent to a current or former landlord asking them to confirm one tenancy from their own records: the dates, the rent, any balance owed, the number of late payments, the notices served, the deposit outcome, and whether they would rent to that tenant again.

faq.question: Who fills out a rental verification form?
faq.answer: The previous landlord or their management company. The requester — a leasing office, a mortgage underwriter, or a housing agency — sends it; the tenant signs the authorization that permits it to be answered; the landlord completes and returns it.

faq.question: Why do rental verification forms come back blank?
faq.answer: Most often because no signed tenant authorization was included, and a management company's standing instruction is to ignore unsigned requests. The next most common reasons are that it went to an individual agent who has left, or that it arrived with no return-by date and no return address.

faq.question: Can a tenant fill out their own rental verification form?
faq.answer: A tenant can pre-fill the tenancy details to save the landlord a lookup, and should sign the authorization. What a tenant cannot do is complete and return the form as though it came from the landlord — the value of the document is that it comes from the landlord's records.

faq.question: How long does rental verification take?
faq.answer: A small landlord often replies in 1 to 3 days. A management company's records office typically takes 5 to 10 days, and a first follow-up call after 5 days is usually what moves it.

faq.question: Is a verification form the same as a credit or screening check?
faq.answer: No. A verification form comes directly from the landlord's own tenancy records. A tenant screening report is a consumer report bought from a screening company and is governed by the Fair Credit Reporting Act, including the notice a landlord owes you if it is used against your application.

/employment-verification-form.heading: Employment Verification Form
/employment-verification-form.lead: An employment verification form is a fixed field sheet an employer completes and returns directly to whoever asked for it. Which form you need is decided by the requester, not by you — a mortgage file, a VA file, and a benefits office each require their own and none accepts a substitute.
/employment-verification-form.shortAnswer: Ask the requester which form they use before filling in anything. Mortgage underwriting uses Fannie Mae Form 1005, a VA loan file uses VA Form 26-8497, a state benefits office has its own, and Form I-9 is not a verification of employment at all.
decisionContext: This page helps you decide which form to obtain before you spend anyone's time on the wrong one. The forms overlap enough to look interchangeable and are treated as anything but by the offices that read them.

It also helps you decide who to ask. Where verification is outsourced to a service, a form emailed to HR is never answered, and the fastest route is to get the employer code to the requester on day one.

Where a verification cannot be obtained at all, the decision becomes what to substitute. Pay stubs and an IRS wage and income transcript are stronger evidence than a form nobody will complete, and both are things you can get yourself.

The generator is free and browser-only. The paid Income + Employment Letter Kit at $59 is the editable download for people who want the verification, the letters, and the income documents as files they keep.

HR and payroll staff completing a verification and unsure what may be released without a signed authorization.
Anyone whose file has been returned as incomplete because the wrong verification form was submitted.

Employer's legal name, worksite address, and the payroll or HR contact who is authorized to verify

commonMistakes: Filling in the form yourself and having your manager sign it. Underwriters and caseworkers are trained to spot an applicant-completed form, and a wrong pay frequency in your own handwriting is worse than a delay.

reviewChecklist: The form is the one the requester named, not a similar form from another program.

steps: Ask the requester which form they use and whether they will accept an alternative. Underwriters and benefits caseworkers usually cannot; landlords and new employers usually can.
Ask your employer how verification is handled before you send anything. If it is outsourced to an automated service, a form emailed to HR will sit unanswered and you will lose a week finding out.
Sign the release first. Send the authorization together with the form, not after payroll has already declined to answer.
Give payroll a return path and a deadline. Name the fax number, secure portal, or email the completed form goes to, and the date it is needed by.
Check the completed form against your own records before it goes out — hire date, title, pay rate, and pay frequency all have to match your pay stubs.
Follow up by phone after 5 business days. The usual cause of a stalled verification is a shared inbox nobody reads, not a refusal.

faq.question: What is an employment verification form?
faq.answer: A structured request that an employer or payroll department completes, confirming employment dates, job title, current status, and — where a signed release exists — hours and pay, returned directly to the party that asked for it rather than to the employee.

faq.question: Which employment verification form do I need?
faq.answer: Whichever one the requester names. A conventional mortgage file uses Fannie Mae Form 1005 or Freddie Mac Form 90, a VA loan file uses VA Form 26-8497, state benefits offices publish their own, and landlords and new employers usually accept anything reasonable. Ask before you send anything.

faq.question: Can I fill out my own employment verification form?
faq.answer: You can pre-fill the factual details to save payroll a lookup, and you should sign the release. What you cannot do is complete it as though it came from the employer — the value of the document is that it comes from payroll records and travels directly to the requester.

faq.question: How long does an employment verification take?
faq.answer: A small employer often replies in 1 to 3 days. A large payroll department typically takes 5 to 10 days, and an automated verification service can answer the same day once the requester has the employer code. A follow-up call after 5 business days is usually what moves a stalled request.

faq.question: Is Form I-9 an employment verification form?
faq.answer: No. Form I-9 records that the employer examined a new hire's identity and work authorization documents. It is retained in the employer's files and is not the document a landlord, lender, or agency is asking for.

faq.question: What if my employer refuses to complete a form?
faq.answer: Many employers have a policy of confirming only dates, title, and status, and of routing anything further to a verification service. Ask which service and pass that on to the requester. Where nothing is available, substitute what you control: recent pay stubs, your W-2, and an IRS wage and income transcript.

Signing it yourself as the employee. It becomes a statement about you rather than a verification of you, which is a different document with much less weight.
Sending it from a personal email address. A letter about employment that arrives from a personal account invites the exact verification call the letter was meant to avoid.
Stating a reason for separation. Most employers have a policy against it, it is almost never asked for, and it can only cost the employee.
reviewChecklist: The letter names one reader and one purpose rather than opening 'to whom it may concern'.
Every figure matches the most recent pay stub, including pay frequency.
Nothing appears about performance, conduct, health, or reason for separation.
Income appears only if the reader asked for it and the employer authorized it.
The signer's direct phone number reaches someone who can confirm what they signed.
steps: Identify the reader first. The whole shape of the letter — how much income detail, whether hours appear, whether a start date alone is enough — follows from who is reading it.
Ask that reader what they require in writing. A leasing office that says a letter is fine will often add, when asked, that it must show gross monthly income.
Take the facts from payroll rather than memory. Title, hire date, and pay frequency all have to survive comparison with a pay stub.
Have it signed by someone with authority to verify. A colleague's signature on company letterhead is worse than a short letter from HR.
Keep it under one page. A verification letter that runs long reads as though it is arguing rather than confirming.
Send it the way the reader asked for it, and keep a copy of what went out and on what date.

faq.question: What should an employment verification letter template include?
faq.answer: At minimum: the employee's full legal name, the employer's legal name, the job title and position type, the hire date, the current status, and an authorized signer with a direct phone number. Compensation, hours, and duties are added only where the specific reader has asked for them.

faq.question: Who should write an employment verification letter?
faq.answer: HR, payroll, or a manager with authority to verify on the employer's behalf. An employee can draft it and send it to HR to correct and sign, which usually speeds things up, but the signature has to come from the employer.

faq.question: Should salary be in the letter?
faq.answer: Only when the reader asked for it and the employer is authorized to disclose it. A landlord and a lender normally need it; a new employer's background check normally does not; and a letter that volunteers it to a reader who did not ask has overshared.

faq.question: Do I need a different template for a landlord and a lender?
faq.answer: Yes, in practice. A leasing office wants gross monthly income and a current-status line. An underwriter wants base pay separated from variable pay and will usually also require a verification form, and a letter that blurs the two invites a follow-up condition.

faq.question: What does a self-employed person send instead?
faq.answer: There is no employer to sign, so the equivalent is a paying client confirming the engagement, sent alongside 1099s, the bank record of the deposits, and where the reader will accept one, a CPA letter. Any single one of those on its own settles very little.

faq.question: How long should the letter be?
faq.answer: One page and usually four to six sentences. A verification letter that runs long reads as though it is arguing a case, and a reviewer who reads an argument starts looking for what is being argued around.

The three lines a leasing office wants will get a mortgage file returned, and the detail an immigration filing needs will make a landlord's copy overshare. /proof-of-employment-letter.heading: Proof of Employment Letter
/proof-of-employment-letter.lead: A proof of employment letter is the weakest item in the employment evidence stack and the easiest one to obtain. This page ranks the eight things reviewers accept as proof, shows where the letter sits among them, and gives you what to attach so the letter holds.
/proof-of-employment-letter.shortAnswer: Send the letter with the two documents that outrank it — a recent pay stub and a W-2 or IRS wage and income transcript — and a reviewer stops having to trust the letter at all. A letter sent alone is a claim; a letter sent with payroll records is corroboration.
decisionContext: This page helps you decide what to send, and in what combination, when someone asks for proof of employment. The ranking of the evidence is the decision; the letter is only one row in it.

It also helps you decide what to do when the letter is unavailable. Two of the three strongest items in the stack can be obtained without your employer's cooperation at all, which changes what a refusal from HR actually costs you.
For a job started this year the decision is how to explain an absence rather than how to fill it. Saying why the W-2 does not exist yet is stronger than hoping nobody looks.
The generator is free and browser-only. The paid Income + Employment Letter Kit at $59 is the editable download for people who want the letters and the packet structure as files they keep.
whoFor: Applicants asked for proof of employment who do not know which documents will satisfy it.
Applicants whose employer will not write a letter or routes everything to a verification service.
People a few months into a new job, where the tax record does not exist yet.
Anyone whose packet came back with a request for something they thought they had already sent.
value: An eight-row ranking of what reviewers actually accept, with the rejection reason for each.
A letter written to reconcile against the pay stub travelling with it, rather than to stand alone.
A cover note that names what is missing and why, which is the part most packets skip.
Two fallback templates: a job started this year, and an employer that will not respond at all.
whatYouGet: A browser-only generator producing the letter and the packet cover note.
The evidence ranking as a comparison table you can work down.
A template for a job with no tax record yet.
A template for sending the payroll and tax record when the employer will not write anything.
Primary sources at the IRS, the FTC, and the Social Security Administration.
useCases: A lender asked for proof of employment and named three acceptable documents.
Your employer confirms nothing in writing and routes verification to an outside service.
You started the job in March and have no W-2 for this employer.
The letter you sent produced a verification call and a week's delay.
A caseworker rejected the packet because the employer name did not match across documents.
prepBrief: Full legal name exactly as payroll and the IRS hold it
Employer's legal name, which is often not the trading name you know
Job title, position type, and date of hire
Current employment status as of the date the packet is sent
Gross pay per pay period and pay frequency, from the stub rather than from memory
Year-to-date gross on the most recent pay stub
The last two W-2 forms, or an IRS wage and income transcript covering the same years
The authorized verifier's name, title, direct phone, and business email
The exact list of what the reviewer said they would accept
commonMistakes: Sending the letter alone. It is the item in the stack a reviewer trusts least, and on its own it produces a verification call and a delay rather than a decision.
Retyping or reformatting a pay stub to make it clearer. A stub that does not look like the payroll system produced it is treated as altered, and the year-to-date arithmetic is checked.
Using the trading name instead of the employer's legal name. When the letter says one name and the W-2 says another, a reviewer has to resolve it, and resolving it takes days.
Offering an offer letter as proof of current employment. It shows a job was offered, not that it started or that it continues.
Staying silent about a document you cannot produce. A reviewer who finds a gap themselves treats it as a gap; a reviewer told about it in advance treats it as a fact of the case.
reviewChecklist: The employer's legal name is identical on the letter, the pay stub, and the W-2.
The year-to-date figure on the newest pay stub is consistent with the pay rate stated in the letter.
The letter carries a direct phone number rather than a general switchboard.
Anything the reviewer listed and you cannot supply is named in the cover note with what you sent in its place.
Nothing in the packet has been retyped, edited, or reformatted from the original.
steps: Ask the reviewer what they accept, in a list. Most will name two or three items, and a packet built to that list is finished on the first pass.
Pull the documents you can get without asking anyone: your last 2 pay stubs from the payroll portal, your last 2 W-2 forms, and an IRS wage and income transcript.

Check that the documents agree with each other before you ask for the letter. If the stub and the W-2 use different employer legal names, explain that in one sentence rather than letting the reviewer find it.
Ask the employer for the letter last, once you know exactly what it needs to say. A letter drafted to match documents you already hold does not need rewriting.
Attach the letter to the records rather than sending it separately. A cover note listing what is enclosed stops a reviewer looking for something you already sent.
Keep a copy of the whole packet and the date it went out. Reviewers lose things, and a resend that is identical to the first is faster than reassembling it.

faq.question: What counts as proof of employment?
faq.answer: Ranked by how reviewers weigh it: an IRS wage and income transcript, pay stubs from the last 30 days, a verification form returned directly by the employer, W-2 forms, an employment verification letter, an offer letter, bank statements showing direct deposit, and last of all a statement you wrote about yourself, which is not evidence.

faq.question: Is a proof of employment letter enough on its own?
faq.answer: Rarely. It is accepted, and then verified by telephone, which costs days. Sent alongside a recent pay stub whose year-to-date figure reconciles with it, the same letter usually closes the question without a call.

faq.question: How do I prove employment for a job I started this year?
faq.answer: The tax record does not exist yet, so the offer letter, the first pay stubs, and a current-status letter have to carry it together. Say plainly in the cover note that no W-2 exists for this employer yet and when the first one will be issued.

faq.question: What if my employer will not give me a letter?
faq.answer: Send the payroll and tax record instead: recent pay stubs, W-2 forms, an IRS wage and income transcript, and bank statements showing the matching deposits. If verification is outsourced, give the reviewer the service name and employer code so they can verify through the route your employer actually uses.

faq.question: Can I write my own proof of employment letter?
faq.answer: You can write it and ask your employer to correct and sign it. What you cannot do is sign it yourself and offer it as proof — a statement you wrote about your own employment is the claim being checked, not evidence for it.

faq.question: Is an automated verification service report the same as a letter?
faq.answer: No, and it is often stronger, because it comes from payroll data rather than from someone typing. It is also a consumer report in this context, so if it is used against your application the Fair Credit Reporting Act gives you the right to be told and to see it.

/letter-of-explanation/template.heading: Letter of Explanation Template
/letter-of-explanation/template.lead: One letter of explanation template, five sentences long, that adapts to any condition you have been asked to explain. Fill it in below and the generator produces the full letter, a short single-question version, and the covering email it travels in.
/letter-of-explanation/template.shortAnswer: A letter of explanation is five sentences: what happened, when, why, what it means now, and what is attached. Everything longer than that is either a second condition that needs its own letter or an argument the reviewer did not ask for.
decisionContext: This page helps you decide what shape the letter takes, which is a different question from what to say. The five parts are the same for every condition; how much of each part a reader needs is not.
It also helps you decide what to leave out, which on this document is where most of the damage happens. A volunteered detail becomes a documented condition.
Where several conditions have been raised, the decision is whether to combine them. Splitting them is almost always right, because conditions clear individually.
The generator is free and browser-only. The $39 Letter of Explanation Kit is the editable download covering nine explanation-letter situations as files you keep.
whoFor: Anyone who has been sent a condition and told to provide a signed letter of explanation.
People who have written one, had it returned, and cannot see what was wrong with it.
People facing several conditions at once who need to know whether to answer them together.
Anyone who needs the structure rather than a story about someone else's situation.
value: One template with a stated structure, rather than a wall of situation-specific samples.
A working generator producing the full letter, a short version, and the covering email.
A reader-by-reader table of what clears the condition and what oversharing looks like for each.
An explicit instruction for the multiple-conditions case, which is where most letters go wrong.
whatYouGet: A browser-only generator with three output documents.
The five-part skeleton as copyable text.
A pattern for answering three conditions without blocking any of them.
A review checklist for the five things that get a letter returned.
Primary sources at the CFPB, Fannie Mae, and Freddie Mac.
useCases: An underwriter has issued a condition requiring a signed letter of explanation.
Your letter was returned and you were not told why.
Three conditions arrived at once and you do not know whether to combine them.
You need to explain something you cannot fully document.
A caseworker wants an explanation covering a specific date range.
prepBrief: The exact wording of the condition, as the reviewer sent it
The reviewer's name, organization, and the file, loan, or case number
What happened, in one sentence, with no adjectives
The dates the event began and ended
The reason, stated plainly and only as far as you can support it
What the position is today, and whether it is resolved
The list of documents attached, with dates, in the order the reviewer should read them
Your full legal name as it appears on the application, and the date you signed
commonMistakes: Paraphrasing the condition instead of quoting it. A processor matching your letter to an open item cannot match a paraphrase, and the letter sits unread.
Covering several conditions in one letter. Each condition is cleared separately in the reviewer's system, and a combined letter blocks all of them until someone unpicks it.
Explaining something nobody asked about. Reviewers are required to document what they learn, so a volunteered issue becomes a new condition.
Sending the letter without the documents named in it, or naming documents that are not attached. Both produce the same result: the condition stays open.
Writing at length. A letter of explanation that runs past a page reads as an argument, and an argument invites scrutiny of what is being argued around.
reviewChecklist: The first line quotes the condition, not your summary of it.
Every date in the letter matches the dates on the attached documents.
There is nothing in the letter about a topic the reviewer did not raise.
Each attachment is named in the letter and actually attached.
It is signed, dated, and carries the file or case number the reviewer uses.
steps: Copy the condition into a blank document first. The letter is built around it, and paraphrasing the condition is the fastest way to answer a question nobody asked.
Write the four facts as four separate lines before you write any prose: what, when, why, where it stands now.
Gather the documents that prove each of those four lines. A fact with nothing behind it either gets removed or gets an explicit note that no document exists for it.
Assemble the five parts in order and stop. Do not add background, apology, or anything about how the application matters to you.
Read it once for anything that could open a new question. Delete that sentence.
Sign it, date it, list the attachments by name and date, and send it by the route the reviewer specified.

faq.question: What should a letter of explanation template include?
faq.answer: Five parts, in order: the condition quoted in the reviewer's own words, what happened and when, why it happened, where the matter stands today, and the documents attached in support. Plus your legal name, the file number, a signature, and a date.

faq.question: How long should a letter of explanation be?
faq.answer: Five to seven sentences for most conditions, and three or four for a narrow one. If it runs past a page, that is usually a sign it is answering more than one condition and should be split.

faq.question: Can one letter cover more than one condition?
faq.answer: It can, but it should not. Conditions are cleared one at a time in the reviewer's system, so a combined letter stays open on all of them until someone separates it. Three conditions means three signed letters and one covering email.

faq.question: Does a letter of explanation need to be signed?
faq.answer: Yes. Most underwriting and benefits workflows treat an unsigned letter as a draft and return it rather than reading it. Sign it, date it, and use the legal name that appears on the application.

faq.question: What if I cannot document part of the explanation?
faq.answer: Say so in the letter, name what does not exist, and offer whatever stands in its place. A reviewer told about a gap in advance treats it as a fact of the case; a reviewer who finds it treats it as a gap.

faq.question: Do I have to use a template at all?
faq.answer: No, but the structure is doing the work. The reviewer is not reading for persuasion — they have one condition to clear and four facts to find. A letter that puts those four facts in a predictable order gets read once.

/letter-of-explanation/mortgage.heading: Letter of Explanation for a Mortgage
/letter-of-explanation/mortgage.lead: Underwriters do not ask for letters of explanation at random. Eight standard conditions generate almost all of them, and each one needs a different set of facts. This page maps the condition wording to what the letter has to contain and what has to travel with it.
/letter-of-explanation/mortgage.shortAnswer: Answer the condition the underwriter wrote, not the topic it belongs to. A letter about your finances in general, sent against a condition about one deposit on one date, does not clear that condition and usually creates a second one.
decisionContext: This page helps you decide which of the eight standard conditions you have been sent, because the condition determines what the letter must contain and what has to travel with it.
It also helps you decide how to split the work. Conditions clear individually, so the decision between one letter and four is really a decision about whether any of them clear this week.
For funds conditions the decision is which records to obtain. The sending side is the one people skip, and it is the side the underwriter is actually asking about.
The generator is free and browser-only. The $99 Loan Prep Letter Kit is the editable download covering the explanation letters and checklists for a full loan file.
whoFor: Borrowers who have received a conditional approval with letters of explanation attached to it.
Borrowers whose letter was returned and who were told only that it was insufficient.
Borrowers facing several conditions at once with a closing date to hold.
Anyone asked about a deposit, an inquiry, an employment gap, or an address that does not reconcile.
value: The eight standard conditions mapped to what actually clears each and what fails.
A generator producing the condition letter, the covering email, and a dedicated credit-inquiry version.
Two full worked templates for the two hardest conditions: employment gap and address history.
Explicit separation of the letter of explanation from the gift letter, which is a routine and expensive confusion.
whatYouGet: A browser-only generator with three outputs, run once per condition.
A condition-to-remedy table you can match your lender's wording against.
Employment gap and address history templates written to condition wording.
A review checklist covering the five reasons letters come back from underwriting.
Primary sources at Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and the IRS.
useCases: Conditional approval arrived with four letters of explanation on the condition list.
The underwriter asked about a deposit and you only have the receiving statement.
You have been asked to explain every credit inquiry in the last 120 days.
There is a gap in your employment history and a closing date to hold.
Your credit file shows an address you cannot immediately document.
prepBrief: The condition identifier and its wording, exactly as the lender issued it
The loan number and the processor or underwriter's name
The account, employer, address, or date the condition names
The dates the event began and ended
The source of any funds involved, and the name of the party they came from
Whether any new debt resulted, stated directly
The current position as of the day you sign
The statements, letters, or records that reconcile against each figure in the letter
commonMistakes: Sending one letter for four conditions. Each has an identifier and clears separately, so a combined letter leaves all four open until a processor separates them.
Answering a source-of-funds condition with only the receiving statement. It shows the money arrived; the underwriter is asking where it came from and whether it is borrowed.
Rounding an amount. A letter saying $8,400 against a statement showing $8,412.63 produces a second request rather than a cleared condition.
Using a letter of explanation where a gift letter is required. They are different documents with different required elements, and the substitution is caught every time.
Explaining an issue the underwriter did not raise. It becomes a documented condition on the file, which is the opposite of what volunteering it was meant to achieve.
reviewChecklist: Each letter names one condition identifier and answers only that condition.
Every amount in the letter matches the statement to the cent.
A funds explanation shows both sides of the transfer, not only the arrival.
A credit inquiry explanation states directly whether new debt resulted.
Nothing in any letter refers to a matter the underwriter did not raise.
steps: Get the condition list from your loan officer in writing. Verbal relays lose the condition identifier, and the identifier is what routes your letter.
Sort the conditions into one letter each, and note which documents each will need before writing anything.

For any funds condition, obtain the record from both sides of the transfer. A statement showing money arriving, with nothing showing it leaving somewhere identifiable, does not close a source-of-funds question.
Write each letter to its condition, quoting the wording, and stop at the point the condition is answered.
Reconcile every figure against the attached statements before you send. A rounded number in the letter against an exact one on the statement causes a second request.
Send them together with one covering email that lists the condition identifiers, and ask the processor to confirm which ones are cleared.

faq.question: Why does a mortgage underwriter want a letter of explanation?
faq.answer: Because the file contains something the documents alone do not settle — a deposit with no visible source, an employment gap, a recent credit inquiry, an address that does not reconcile. It is issued as a condition, which means the loan cannot be cleared to close until it is answered.

faq.question: What are the most common mortgage letter of explanation requests?
faq.answer: Eight cover almost all of them: a large deposit, credit inquiries within the last 120 days, late payments, an employment gap, an address history discrepancy, a name variation, NSF or overdraft activity, and gift funds.

faq.question: How do I explain a large deposit to an underwriter?
faq.answer: Show both sides of the transfer. Name the sender and your relationship to them, attach the statement from the sending account and the receiving statement, and state directly that the funds are not borrowed and no repayment is owed.

faq.question: Do I need one letter or several?
faq.answer: One per condition. Conditions are tracked and cleared individually, so a single letter covering several of them stays open on all of them until someone unpicks it. Send them together with one covering email listing the identifiers.

faq.question: Is a letter of explanation the same as a gift letter?
faq.answer: No. A gift letter has specific required elements — the donor, the relationship, the amount, and an express statement that no repayment is expected — and lenders will not accept a general explanation in its place.

faq.question: Will a letter of explanation get my mortgage approved?
faq.answer: No. It clears one condition. The credit decision rests on income, assets, the debt-to-income calculation, the appraisal, and the lender's own overlays, none of which any letter can change.
